introduction.p: If f is differentiable at a, the tangent line gives the local approximation f(x)\approx f(a)+f\prime(a)(x-a). We will describe how the approximation error behaves as x\to a and use it to estimate changes in function values.

subsection.p: The tangent line does not equal the curve except at the point of tangency. But near that point, the line and the curve are close.

exercise.title: Why can a tangent line replace a curve nearby?

statement.p: Near a point of tangency, calculus lets us replace a curved graph by a line. In your own words, why is that replacement useful, and why does it fail if we wander too far from the point?

hint.p: A line is simple, and differentiability says the curve and its tangent stay close under enough magnification. Distance from the point of tangency is what the approximation depends on.

exercise.title: Why does differentiability mean the error is small compared with h?

statement.p: If f is differentiable at a, then f(a+h)=f(a)+f'(a)h+E(h) with E(h)/h\to 0. In your own words, why is that stronger than merely saying the error goes to 0, and why does |x| fail this test at the origin?

hint.p: The error must shrink faster than the input step. A corner would require two different first-order slopes at once.

exercise.title: Why is dy not the same as \Delta y?

statement.p: The differential dy=f'(x)\,dx is the change predicted by the tangent line, while \Delta y is the exact change along the curve. In your own words, why do those two quantities differ, and why does a large |f'(x)| make a small input error dangerous?

hint.p: One quantity follows the line; the other follows the curve. The derivative is the local conversion factor from input change to output change.

subsection.p: Local linear approximation is one of the main reasons derivatives matter. A differentiable function may be curved, but under enough magnification it behaves like a line.

That raises the next question. If a function has a derivative at a point, what does that force the original function to do near that point? In particular, can a differentiable function jump? The answer is no, and the reason is hidden inside the same local linear formula.
